data.sourceWord: MCQ: Definition of an extended family
data.targetWord: An extended family consists of parents living with their children and grandparents — and potentially other relatives such as aunts and uncles — under the same household or in close proximity. This is distinct from a nuclear family (parents and children only).

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.1 (1 mark) — Answer: D Parents living with children and grandparents

data.targetWord: Many religions teach that sexuality is a fundamental part of being human, created by God as a natural aspect of human identity. Because sexuality is God-given, it is seen as sacred and should be expressed in a responsible, respectful way that honours human dignity.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 (2 marks) — Give two religious beliefs about human sexuality

data.sourceWord: Religious belief: Heterosexuality as traditional norm
data.targetWord: Most traditional religious teachings view heterosexuality as the norm for sexual relationships, believing marriage between a man and woman is divinely ordained. However, many believers also accept that sexuality can be fluid and that people may express it in different ways, requiring pastoral sensitivity.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 (2 marks) — Give two religious beliefs about human sexuality

data.sourceWord: Contrasting belief: Islam permits limited polygamy
data.targetWord: Islam permits polygamy under certain conditions according to Shari'ah law — a man may marry up to four wives if he treats them all equally, seeks consent of his first wife, and financially supports each one. This was originally permitted to protect war widows and vulnerable women.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.3 (4 marks) — Contrasting religious beliefs about polygamy

data.targetWord: Christians are generally against polygamy, believing marriage is an exclusive covenant between two people: 'a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife and they shall become one flesh.' (Genesis 2:24). Each person should have one spouse: 'each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.' (1 Corinthians 7:2).

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.3 (4 marks) — Contrasting religious beliefs about polygamy

data.sourceWord: FOR: Marriage is not important today — changing social norms
data.targetWord: In contemporary society, many couples cohabit without marrying and raise families successfully outside of marriage. Changing social attitudes mean fewer people see marriage as necessary for a committed relationship, and legal rights for cohabiting couples have increased — suggesting marriage is no longer essential.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Marriage is not important in today's world'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Marriage remains important — religious covenant
data.targetWord: For religious believers, marriage is a sacred covenant made before God that provides the foundation for family life. Christians, Muslims, Jews and Sikhs all have religious marriage ceremonies emphasising lifelong commitment. The stability marriage provides for raising children and building communities means it remains deeply important.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Marriage is not important in today's world'

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Term for the belief that human life is sacred
data.targetWord: Sanctity of life — the belief that human life is holy and has intrinsic value because it is created by God. This principle underpins many religious views on abortion, euthanasia, and capital punishment, as taking human life is seen as violating something sacred.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.1 (1 mark) — Answer: D Sanctity of life

data.sourceWord: FOR: Religious believers should oppose abortion — sanctity argument
data.targetWord: Many religious believers oppose abortion because human life is sacred and begins at conception, created in God's image. Killing an innocent human being — even an unborn one — violates the sanctity of life. 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you' (Jeremiah 1:5) supports the view that God values life from conception.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Religious believers should be against abortion'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Some religious believers permit abortion — compassion argument
data.targetWord: Some religious traditions permit abortion in certain circumstances, emphasising compassion for the mother. Liberal Christians and Reform Jews argue that the quality of life of an already-living woman may outweigh the potential life of a foetus, especially in cases of rape, foetal abnormality, or risk to the mother's life.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Religious believers should be against abortion'

data.sourceWord: MCQ: What is NOT an example of General Revelation?
data.targetWord: Being told about God by other people is NOT General Revelation — this is Special Revelation (direct, personal communication). General Revelation includes experiencing awe at a sunset, seeing evidence of design in nature, or having a religious experience — ways God reveals himself to all people through creation.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q3.1 (1 mark) — Answer: A Being told about God by other people

data.sourceWord: FOR: Design argument does NOT prove God — Darwinian challenge
data.targetWord: Darwin's theory of natural selection provides a non-religious explanation for the apparent design in nature — complex organisms evolved through random mutation and survival of the fittest, not divine creation. This suggests that apparent design is an illusion, undermining the Design Argument's claim that an intelligent creator is necessary.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q3.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'The Design argument does not prove that God exists'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Design argument points to God — fine-tuning
data.targetWord: The fine-tuning of the universe's fundamental constants (gravity, electromagnetism) to support life is statistically improbable by chance. Paley's watchmaker analogy argues that just as a watch implies a watchmaker, the complexity and order of the universe implies an intelligent designer — namely God.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q3.5 (12 marks) — Arguments supporting the Design Argument as evidence for God

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Belief that all violence is wrong
data.targetWord: Pacifism — the belief that all violence and war is morally wrong and that conflicts should be resolved through peaceful means. Pacifists refuse to participate in war or violent action. Many religious believers, including Quakers and some Buddhists, hold pacifist views based on sacred teachings about peace.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q4.1 (1 mark) — Answer: C Pacifism

data.sourceWord: FOR: Self-defence is the only just reason for war
data.targetWord: Many religious traditions accept war only in genuine self-defence. Just War theory (developed by Aquinas) requires war to be a last resort, have a just cause, and protect the innocent. Islam permits jihad in defence of the community. Waging war for any other reason — conquest, resources — cannot be religiously justified.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q4.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'Self-defence is the only good reason for going to war'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Other just reasons for war exist
data.targetWord: Just War theory also permits war to protect innocent civilians from oppression (humanitarian intervention), to restore peace and order, or to prevent greater evil. The UN Charter permits military action to prevent genocide. Religious thinkers argue that standing by while innocents are slaughtered is also a moral failure.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q4.5 (12 marks) — Arguments against 'self-defence is the only reason for war'
